completionCriteria: Porting rule 1: understand and preserve the original tests intent, preconditions and ability to detect defects. Preserve inputs, expected results, assertions, state transitions, ownership, execution order, concurrency boundaries, helper structure and explanatory comments. Do not weaken, merge away or replace these contracts to fit the CLR implementation or increase counts. Make only necessary Java-to-CLR adaptations, record their reason and establish equivalent validation. Keep individually named PascalCase tests traceable to the original; additional CLR regressions remain separately identifiable.
Every reviewed contract has an implemented counterpart or an explicit CLR/JVM-only decision; unreviewed is not counted as missing.
Ownership, indices/marks, failure effects and relevant virtual dispatch agree with the original or have an explicit consumer-supported CLR adaptation.
Reuse existing contract/differential evidence; add regression tests for confirmed gaps or uncovered required contracts, not merely to increase counts.
Preserve original comments beside the implementation or as explicit references when the obsolete API itself is replaced.
Validate net10.0 Debug, Release and rebuilt checked Release with SIMPLE sampling interval 1 for runtime changes; preserve unrelated workspace edits.
Decide module completion from source/consumer contracts; the complete original Java fixture count is not the sole gate.

Completion review: the abstract ByteBuf contract has all 192 declared public methods accounted for, its twelve concrete default methods and sole internal isAccessible helper map to existing CLR implementations, and its three implemented interfaces map to IReferenceCounted, IComparable<ByteBuf> and IByteBufConvertible. There are no original fields/constructors or additional source operations in this abstract class. JVM-only API comments remain explicit references rather than dummy compatibility members. Component-scalar update: the bounded CLR byte/word storage kernels are internally virtual, preserving composite component-public dispatch through optimized ordinary/read-only/pooled views without invoking the view parent public primitive override. Default contiguous storage still uses Memory/Span/BinaryPrimitives. Public APIs and existing representation/permission/reference policies are unchanged; full policy and regression evidence are in docs/buffer-porting.md#component-scalar-storage-dispatch. Bulk update: a physically contiguous borrow from a composite no longer bypasses its logical component transfer kernel. Span and ByteBuf requests select their corresponding component overloads; mutable Copy uses the original private typed-copy loop. Aliased ranges keep the existing CLR snapshot policy, with scratch peers only for alias handling. Physical overlap inspection traverses internal borrowed sequences and transparent views without public memory-access/leak records. Opaque aggregate sources use the existing CLR span storage kernel where the receiver controls the transfer. I/O keeps its documented staged span policy. Iteration/search update: internal ascending/descending loops consume bounded scalar storage kernels rather than physical spans. Mutable composites peel transparent/sliced/pooled component storage before internal iteration, bypass public component iteration overrides and translate stop indices; read-only component storage and inherited readable view loops keep their distinct scalar behavior. Reverse scans are bounded by captured component offsets (an intentional correction of the pinned source defect). Indexed view/facade delegation, CLR guards, exception identity and cursor/claim rules remain. Byte search retains the Span fast path on direct storage and uses logical scalar kernels on aggregates; pattern search materializes aggregate logical GetByte values before Span.IndexOf. This is a CLR linear-byte/materialization strategy, without SWAR/Two-Way callback-width, O(1)-space or performance equivalence. Pooled views propagate segmented TryGetMemory/TryGetReadOnlyMemory and Span-write/zero kernels to their translated root instead of requiring contiguous memory.

array-spans.adaptation: Java whole-array and offset/length overload pairs collapse into four virtual CLR operations: GetBytes/ReadBytes with Span<byte>, SetBytes/WriteBytes with ReadOnlySpan<byte>. Null arrays become valid empty spans; requesting a nonempty range from null fails, matching the existing documented CLR policy. A span has no array position/limit or ownership claim. Absolute transfers preserve both buffer indices; relative reads/writes advance only their respective cursor after a successful copy. Read dispatches through virtual GetBytes; Write through public EnsureWritable and virtual SetBytes, with a CLR memory lease protecting aliased native storage across growth. clr-text-encoding.adaptation: Charset becomes caller-supplied Encoding; immutable CLR strings replace String/CharSequence/AsciiString decode results, and ReadOnlySpan<char> replaces CharSequence input. GetString has readable-window and indexed capacity-bounded forms; ReadString enforces readable bytes and advances only after successful decode, unlike current Java readCharSequence/readString implementations which use absolute decoding without an explicit readable check. SetString does not grow or change indices; WriteString reserves Encoding.GetByteCount exact length, not the Java UTF8 pessimistic char-count*3 reservation, then commits writer after success. Encoding controls strict/replacement fallback and wire bytes. Java UTF16 maps to explicit big-endian Encoding in these fixtures; GetBytes does not automatically emit its BOM (512 vs Java 514 bytes for 256 chars). ASCII Encoding emits fallback ? for é, whereas Netty specialized ASCII writes/decodes preserve byte E9; Java and CLR wire bytes are deliberately not equated. Preamble/BOM framing belongs to callers; use ByteBufUtil.WriteUtf8/WriteAscii when the existing Netty-specific byte policy is required. Native leases preserve aliased text across growth. Existing custom-encoding and wrapper forwarding contracts remain.

clr-nio-transfer-completion.adaptation: NIO ByteBuffer transfer regions become Span<byte>/ReadOnlySpan<byte>. Callers select the former position-to-limit region with a slice; spans have no mutable NIO cursor. clr-io-completion.adaptation: OutputStream/InputStream use Stream; connected GatheringByteChannel/ScatteringByteChannel use Socket; positioned FileChannel uses SafeFileHandle with RandomAccess. EOF is CLR zero rather than Java -1. Socket calls return actual counts, synchronous WouldBlock becomes zero; Stream input reads once and Stream output writes the whole span or throws. RandomAccess writes the whole requested range or throws and preserves handle position; Java permits partial file writes. Absolute indices stay unchanged; relative indices publish successful counts, growth can survive EOF/failure, and borrowed resources remain caller-owned. referenceComments: // Determine reasonable default for nHeapArena and nDirectArena.
// Assuming each arena has 3 chunks, the pool should not consume more than 50% of max memory.

/*
         * We use 2 * available processors by default to reduce contention as we use 2 * available processors for the
         * number of EventLoops in NIO and EPOLL as well. If we choose a smaller number we will run into hot spots as
         * allocation and de-allocation needs to be synchronized on the PoolArena.
         *
         * See https://github.com/netty/netty/issues/3888.
         */
// Use 1023 by default as we use an ArrayDeque as backing storage which will then allocate an internal array
// of 1024 elements. Otherwise we would allocate 2048 and only use 1024 which is wasteful.

/**
     * Default control creation of PoolThreadCache finalizers for FastThreadLocalThreads -

     */

referenceComments:
/** * Abstraction of a byte buffer - the fundamental data structure * to represent a low-level binary and text message. * * Netty uses its own buffer API instead of NIO {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer} to * represent a sequence of bytes. This approach has significant advantage over * using {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer}. Netty's new buffer type, * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf}, has been designed from ground * up to address the problems of {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer} and to meet the * daily needs of network application developers. To list a few cool features: *
    *
  • You can define your buffer type if necessary.
    • *
  • Transparent zero copy is achieved by built-in composite buffer type.
    • *
  • A dynamic buffer type is provided out-of-the-box, whose capacity is * expanded on demand, just like {@link java.lang.StringBuffer}.
    • *
  • There's no need to call the {@code flip()} method anymore.
    • *
  • It is often faster than {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer}.
    • *
* *

Extensibility

* * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} has rich set of operations * optimized for rapid protocol implementation. For example, * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} provides various operations * for accessing unsigned values and strings and searching for certain byte * sequence in a buffer. You can also extend or wrap existing buffer type * to add convenient accessors. The custom buffer type still implements * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} interface rather than * introducing an incompatible type. * *

Transparent Zero Copy

* * To lift up the performance of a network application to the extreme, you need * to reduce the number of memory copy operation. You might have a set of * buffers that could be sliced and combined to compose a whole message. Netty * provides a composite buffer which allows you to create a new buffer from the * arbitrary number of existing buffers with no memory copy. For example, a * message could be composed of two parts; header and body. In a modularized * application, the two parts could be produced by different modules and * assembled later when the message is sent out. * 
 * +--------+----------+
 * | header |   body   |
 * +--------+----------+
 *
* If {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer} were used, you would have to create a new big * buffer and copy the two parts into the new buffer. Alternatively, you can * perform a gathering write operation in NIO, but it restricts you to represent * the composite of buffers as an array of {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer}s rather * than a single buffer, breaking the abstraction and introducing complicated * state management. Moreover, it's of no use if you are not going to read or * write from an NIO channel. * 
 * // The composite type is incompatible with the component type.
 * ByteBuffer[] message = new ByteBuffer[] { header, body };
 *
* By contrast, {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} does not have such * caveats because it is fully extensible and has a built-in composite buffer * type. * 
 * // The composite type is compatible with the component type.
 * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} message = {@link io.netty.buffer.Unpooled}.wrappedBuffer(header, body);
 *
 * // Therefore, you can even create a composite by mixing a composite and an
 * // ordinary buffer.
 * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} messageWithFooter = {@link io.netty.buffer.Unpooled}.wrappedBuffer(message, footer);
 *
 * // Because the composite is still a {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf}, you can access its content
 * // easily, and the accessor method will behave just like it's a single buffer
 * // even if the region you want to access spans over multiple components.  The
 * // unsigned integer being read here is located across body and footer.
 * messageWithFooter.getUnsignedInt(
 *     messageWithFooter.readableBytes() - footer.readableBytes() - 1);
 *
* *

Automatic Capacity Extension

* * Many protocols define variable length messages, which means there's no way to * determine the length of a message until you construct the message or it is * difficult and inconvenient to calculate the length precisely. It is just * like when you build a {@link java.lang.String}. You often estimate the length * of the resulting string and let {@link java.lang.StringBuffer} expand itself * on demand. * 
 * // A new dynamic buffer is created.  Internally, the actual buffer is created
 * // lazily to avoid potentially wasted memory space.
 * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} b = {@link io.netty.buffer.Unpooled}.buffer(4);
 *
 * // When the first write attempt is made, the internal buffer is created with
 * // the specified initial capacity (4).
 * b.writeByte('1');
 *
 * b.writeByte('2');
 * b.writeByte('3');
 * b.writeByte('4');
 *
 * // When the number of written bytes exceeds the initial capacity (4), the
 * // internal buffer is reallocated automatically with a larger capacity.
 * b.writeByte('5');
 *
* *

Better Performance

* * Most frequently used buffer implementation of * {@link io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf} is a very thin wrapper of a * byte array (i.e. {@code byte[]}). Unlike {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer}, it has * no complicated boundary check and index compensation, and therefore it is * easier for a JVM to optimize the buffer access. More complicated buffer * implementation is used only for sliced or composite buffers, and it performs * as well as {@link java.nio.ByteBuffer}. */

No mutable scratch NIO cursor or permanent raw address API is introduced.
